units.title: UNIT 5: Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing

outcomes.text: Identify the main types of taxes individuals pay.
Individuals may pay federal, state, and local income, capital gains, payroll, property, and sales taxes.
Income taxes are based on earnings; employers usually withhold employee taxes, while self-employed people submit their own.
Capital gains taxes apply to profits from selling assets and generally use a separate, lower rate than income taxes.
Payroll taxes support programs such as Social Security and Medicare; employers share these payments, while self-employed workers pay all.
Property taxes depend on the value of possessions such as homes, land, and vehicles and may be paid periodically.
Sales taxes are calculated from purchase prices, collected by sellers, and remitted to the government.
Explain why federal income-tax amounts differ among individuals and households.
Income, deductions, and credits affect the federal income tax an individual or household owes.
The progressive federal tax system generally applies higher rates to higher-income earners.
Tax deductions lower taxable income; examples include eligible mortgage interest, retirement contributions, donations, taxes, and medical expenses.
Tax credits directly reduce taxes owed and may cover children, care, education, or qualifying purchases.
Determine and explain the parts of an individual’s pay stub.
A pay stub shows gross earnings, required and optional deductions, and net pay.
Gross income is total pay for a period, determined by salary, hours, contracts, or another compensation method.
Mandatory deductions, including income and payroll taxes, are required by law and withheld by employers.
Voluntary deductions fund benefits such as health coverage, care accounts, life insurance, retirement savings, and union dues.
Pretax deductions reduce taxable income and can encourage saving by lowering tax liability.
Net pay is earnings remaining after all deductions and can differ substantially from gross income.
Identify insurable risks individuals may encounter.
People face financial and physical risks, including accidents and illnesses that can impair their ability to work.
Insurable risks are chance-based, measurable, and statistically predictable potential losses.
Personal risk concerns insurable threats to an individual’s health or well-being.
Property risk concerns potential damage or loss involving an insured person’s belongings, home, or vehicle.
Liability risk involves harming another person’s property or physical well-being.
Describe insurance types individuals use to limit financial losses.
Health, auto, homeowners, renters, and life insurance protect against different insurable financial losses.
Policyholders pay premiums for selected coverage and can submit claims after covered losses.
Health insurance helps pay for necessary medical care and may be partly employer-funded.
Auto, homeowners, and renters insurance may reimburse property losses and liability costs.
Life insurance pays beneficiaries after the insured’s death to replace income or meet future financial needs.
Extended warranties and service contracts can provide insurance-like protection for costly purchases.
Recommend insurance coverage suited to a household’s needs and willingness to accept risk.
Coverage needs depend on legal requirements, risk tolerance, and the number of dependents.
Some coverage is legally required; for example, states commonly require auto liability insurance and mortgage lenders require property insurance.
Lower-risk-tolerance individuals may choose broader coverage and higher premiums, while others may accept higher deductibles and out-of-pocket costs.
People with dependents may need additional health, vehicle, and life insurance protection.
Safer behavior, such as careful driving or avoiding smoking, can lower insurance premiums.
False information or claims by policyholders or insurers constitute criminal insurance fraud.
Explain ways individuals and households can guard against financial fraud.
Predatory lending, phishing, identity theft, and online scams create personal and financial risks.
Compare lenders, resist pressure, and consult nonprofit credit counselors before accepting loan terms.
Assess offer credibility, protect personal information, freeze credit when needed, and seek legal help after scams.
Explain how financial planning helps achieve education, housing, retirement, and charitable-giving goals.
Long-term goals may include funding education, purchasing a home, saving for retirement, and giving to charity.
Education choices depend on career aims and funding, commonly combining savings, loans, scholarships, grants, and work-study.
Housing choices depend on preferences and resources; buying usually combines a down payment with a mortgage whose payments vary by loan terms.

units.title: UNIT 1: Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas

outcomes.text: Explain how personal and organizational values and capabilities influence decisions.
Core values are fundamental beliefs that direct an individual’s or business’s behavior.
Businesses express their values to unite employees and guide decisions toward a common purpose.
Core competencies are distinctive capabilities, skills, and expertise that help achieve competitive advantage.
Businesses use their strengths to select opportunities and direct resources toward satisfying customers.
Individuals use their values and abilities to evaluate education, career, and employment options.
Create or assess vision and mission statements using organizational goals and values.
Describe a vision statement as a concise summary of values and future aspirations.
Describe a mission statement as what a business does and how it pursues long-term goals.
Explain how vision and mission statements guide decisions and communicate goals to stakeholders.
Describe the purposes of businesses, social enterprises, and nonprofit organizations.
Explain that businesses pursue profitability, missions, goals, competitiveness, and long-term viability.
Describe social enterprises as organizations combining profit-seeking with social objectives.
Explain that nonprofits serve the public good, reinvest surplus, and often depend on grants and donations.
Identify how businesses address customer problems, needs, and wants.
A business produces and distributes goods or services, regardless of its size or customer reach.
A customer buys a product, while a consumer uses it; these may be different people.
Businesses identify market opportunities, create solutions, and choose which customers and needs to serve.
Distinguish between creating value for customers and capturing value through pricing.
Value is the benefit or worth customers assign to a product.
Businesses create value by offering products that address customer problems, needs, or wants.
Businesses capture value when their selling price exceeds production cost.
Explain how sellers and buyers interact to establish market prices.
Markets are physical or virtual settings where businesses and customers exchange products.
Voluntary exchange generates seller revenue and gives buyers needed or desired products.
Sellers seek higher prices and profits, while buyers seek lower prices and savings.
Competition between sellers and buyers tends to establish a prevailing market price.
Develop or assess a business plan for achieving competitive advantage.
Competitive advantage enables a business to outperform rivals, increasing market share and potentially profits.
Market competitiveness depends on rivals, product differences, and competitors’ ability to offer lower prices.
A market’s competitiveness influences the strategies businesses use to gain advantage.
Commodity businesses may seek advantage through efficiency that permits the lowest possible prices.
Businesses with differentiated products can compete through quality, features, service, price, or marketing.
Businesses may build entry barriers through patents, regulations, supplier access, startup costs, or scale.
A monopoly has one seller and may preserve its position by maintaining entry barriers.
Describe political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal market factors.
PESTEL factors shape the business environment and determine which businesses can succeed in a market.
Political factors include policies and political conditions affecting trade, taxes, subsidies, mandates, bans, and stability.
Economic factors include stability, income, inflation, unemployment, and interest rates affecting market activity.
Social factors include demographics, cultural norms, lifestyles, and population trends influencing consumers and markets.
Technological factors include technology availability, internet access, automation, and innovation affecting market activity.
Environmental factors include geography, resources, waste policies, and customer environmental attitudes.
Legal factors include employment, consumer protection, safety, environmental, intellectual property, and antitrust regulations.
Explain how PESTEL factors affect business viability and career opportunities.
Political systems and policies encourage some business activities and discourage others through taxes, subsidies, mandates, and bans.
Economic conditions affect spending, so businesses may thrive in either strong or weak economies depending on customer needs.
Social demographics, norms, and trends shape consumer needs and business viability.
Available technology affects production, distribution, and communication, influencing business viability.
Climate, resources, disasters, and environmental preferences can constrain operations and influence purchases.
Laws and regulations affect operating costs and whether particular business activities are legal.
Career opportunities depend partly on which businesses are viable in a location.
Changes in PESTEL factors can alter business conditions and local job availability.
Apply PESTEL analysis to judge a market’s attractiveness and risks.
Businesses assess relevant PESTEL factors and their effects on a product’s or business idea’s market prospects and risks.
Businesses are more likely to enter markets whose PESTEL conditions fit their models, resources, processes, and customers.
Changing PESTEL factors can affect customers, operations, distribution, resources, and a business’s viability.
Describe methods entrepreneurs and businesses use to create new product ideas.
An entrepreneur creates a business while accepting its risks and possible rewards.
Businesses generate ideas by observing, interviewing, surveying, researching gaps, and experimenting with new capabilities.
Explain new-product risks and why entrepreneurs and businesses accept them.
New products require costly financial, physical, and human resources without guaranteeing sufficient revenue or profit.
Potential profits, solving problems, and pursuing passions can motivate businesses to accept new-product risks.
Use entrepreneurial design thinking to create and validate a business or product idea.
Use observation, interviews, and surveys to verify that a clearly defined problem affects multiple potential customers.
After validating a problem, develop a solution through brainstorming, sketching, and prototyping.
Test an initial product idea by collecting customer feedback on a simple minimum viable product.
Explain how and why businesses promote ethical conduct.
Explain how unethical conduct and incentive systems can encourage people to pursue personal benefits improperly.
Identify ways businesses promote ethics, including codes, training, consequences, and leadership example.
Explain how ethical practices affect customer loyalty, employee relationships, reputation, and profitability.
Explain how leaders address ethical dilemmas.
Define an ethical dilemma as a conflict among values or between values and business goals.
Explain how leaders consider stakeholders, reputation, and company culture when responding to ethical dilemmas.
Explain how leaders choose responses by weighing stakeholder effects or following organizational values and goals.
Describe major business structures and compare their advantages and disadvantages.
Identify sole proprietorships, partnerships, LLCs, and corporations as major business structures.
Explain how unincorporated structures and LLCs preserve owner control but may limit growth funding.
Compare personal liability for sole proprietors and partners with the liability protection of LLCs.
Explain how corporations trade owner control for greater funding, growth potential, and separate business liability.
Define sole proprietors’ and partners’ roles and responsibilities.
Explain that sole proprietors manage all business areas and may perform several specialized roles.
Explain that partners share broad responsibilities and typically divide roles by strengths and interests.
Explain why large businesses use specialized departments, leadership, management, and outsourcing.
Explain that growth and complexity lead businesses to assign responsibilities to specialized teams.
Describe executive leaders’ and managers’ responsibilities and reporting relationships in large businesses.
Explain how specialized departments build expertise and improve efficient, effective service to customers.
Explain why businesses outsource activities to improve efficiency, reduce costs, or obtain missing expertise.
Describe specialized departments’ purposes, responsibilities, and roles.
Explain how sales and marketing attract and retain customers through research, selling, branding, and relationships.
Explain how research and development improves goods, services, and processes through innovation.
Describe how operations manage production or service delivery processes.
Explain how accounting tracks financial activity and prepares statements to assess business health.
Explain how finance obtains and manages funds and recommends performance improvements using financial data.
Describe how human resources recruits, trains, and evaluates employees for business needs.
Describe factors businesses consider when designing production processes.
Compare artisan production, which relies on skilled labor, with technology-intensive mass production.
Explain how customer priorities, capabilities, and competition influence production-process choices.
Develop or describe a product supply-chain plan.
Explain how supply chains connect participants from raw-material acquisition through customer delivery.
Describe how goods move from materials and components through manufacturing, storage, distribution, and retail.
Describe service supply chains involving employees, resources, and systems for in-person or virtual delivery.
Explain how cost, quality, efficiency, convenience, and risks affect supplier selection.
Explain how competitive strategy influences supply-chain choices.
Explain how low-price strategies favor mass production, cost reduction, and scalable supply chains.
Explain how quality-focused businesses select high-quality resources and production methods.
Explain how entry barriers can involve exclusive supplier or distributor agreements.
Explain why marketers gather customer information and how they use it.
Marketing includes identifying customer problems, needs, and wants, then promoting, selling, and delivering products.
Customer information helps businesses choose whom to serve, what to offer, and how to market profitably.
Marketers gather customer information about demographic and psychographic characteristics.
Businesses obtain customer information through digital tools, traditional research, and purchases from other companies.
Use market segmentation to find target customers and create customer profiles.
Market segmentation groups potential customers by shared demographic and psychographic traits to reveal differing needs.
Target customers are the buyers most likely to purchase because of their needs, wants, and preferences.
A customer profile is a fictional representative containing target customers’ demographic, psychographic, and preference information.
Targeting and profiling help businesses design more appealing and cost-effective products and marketing.
Explain why customer relationships matter and plan ways to strengthen them.
Businesses build relationships through personalized service, rewards, feedback, social media, and internet-based interactions.
Strong relationships can lower customer acquisition costs and raise profits through customer referrals.
Strong relationships can increase customer lifetime value through loyalty and repeat purchases.
Explain how customer-data practices can expose consumers and businesses to privacy, identity-theft, and fraud risks.
Collecting and storing personal information may violate privacy, especially without clear customer awareness or consent.
Poorly protected customer information can enable data breaches, fraud, and identity theft.
Businesses must weigh data-use benefits against customer loss, value conflicts, reputational damage, and other risks.
Explain why and how consumers decide what to buy.
Consumers purchase goods and services for needs and wants; price, features, availability, and advertising affect choices.
Some purchases involve systematic comparison, while smaller purchases are often habitual; rational evaluation requires time and information.
Age, education, income, budget, occupation, and lifestyle influence consumers’ needs, wants, and ability to pay.
Values, beliefs, perceptions, learned associations, and motivations shape attitudes toward products and willingness to buy.
Peers, family, social status, cultural norms, and media influence what consumers consider acceptable or desirable.
Store conditions, timing, and product availability create temporary influences that encourage or discourage purchases.
Describe how legal and technological changes affect consumer purchasing patterns.
Purchasing patterns describe consumers’ usual timing, frequency, and quantities, influenced by location, income, family, and friends.
Laws shape purchasing by restricting products or transaction conditions and may encourage substitute products.
Technology and innovation introduce products and shopping methods that change how consumers meet needs and wants.
Evaluate Cialdini-based sales approaches and create an appropriate sales tactic.
Cialdini’s influence principles explain psychological reasons people comply; marketers use them to encourage purchases.
Scarcity tactics increase desire by making products seem rare or available for only a limited time.
Authority tactics use experts or credentials to make consumers more likely to follow recommendations.
Consensus tactics use favorable customer feedback to suggest that many people approve of a product.
Liking tactics feature relatable people and personal rapport to make consumers more receptive.
Reciprocity tactics provide samples, trials, or gifts that encourage recipients to respond with a purchase.
Consistency tactics connect products with consumers’ self-images and encourage behavior aligned with their identities.
Unity tactics build group identity or community, making members more receptive to influence.
Explain why businesses perform market research.
Market research gathers detailed information about markets, products, and customer behavior to guide marketing decisions.
Market researchers collect both numerical and descriptive information.
New-product businesses research desirability, feasibility, and viability before committing substantial resources.
Explain how existing businesses use research to understand changing needs, identify innovations, and retain or expand market share.
Conduct and interpret secondary research to evaluate a market opportunity.
Explain how secondary and primary research reveal customers, competitors, market conditions, and PESTEL influences.
Describe secondary research sources and the market information they provide, including size, trends, segments, and customer influences.
Explain why businesses interpret secondary research, including competitor information, when assessing a product opportunity.
Conduct and interpret primary research testing hypotheses about target customers and their preferences.
Describe primary research methods businesses use to test customer and preference hypotheses.
Define a business hypothesis and explain why businesses test assumptions before acting.
Explain how needed data determines the choice or combination of primary research methods.
Explain when surveys are appropriate for collecting extensive quantitative data representing a population.
Explain when focus groups and interviews provide detailed qualitative insights from a small number of people.
Explain how experiments and observations measure customer behavior in controlled or natural settings.
Explain how A/B testing compares authentic customer responses to two viable alternatives.
Explain how representative samples and unbiased questions reduce skewed research data.
Recognize that businesses must often decide amid limited, unclear, or contradictory research because predictions can be inaccurate.
Develop and interpret visualizations that communicate market research findings.
Explain how visualizations reveal and communicate patterns, trends, and insights for evidence-based decisions.
Choose the visualization that best communicates a desired pattern, trend, or insight.
Explain that bar charts compare individual data points, such as sales or business revenues.
Explain that stacked bar charts compare totals and their component categories.
Explain that line graphs show changes and trends over time.
Explain that pie charts show how parts comprise a whole.
Describe product development’s six stages and create an MVP and value proposition.
Identify product development’s six stages: ideation, validation, design, messaging, production, and launch.
Explain how ideation generates product ideas through research, development, and brainstorming.
Explain how validation tests ideas with customers and uses MVPs to assess product-market fit.
Describe how design develops prototypes, evaluates costs and features, and incorporates customer feedback.
Explain how messaging creates marketing strategy, value propositions, and positioning relative to competitors.
Explain how production builds the product, incorporates feedback, establishes supply chains, and aligns output with demand.
Explain how launch begins customer ordering, distribution, and marketing to the target segment.
Develop and evaluate branding for a business or product.
Explain how branding distinguishes products, builds awareness, and encourages customer loyalty.
Explain how vision and value propositions guide brand identities appealing to target customers.
Identify brand identity elements and explain how trademarks protect them.
Explain why businesses may offer generic products to customers prioritizing lower costs over branding.
Explain how marketing strategies adapt to competitive challenges during the product life cycle.
Define the product life cycle as stages from introduction through decline shaped by changing demand.
Explain how businesses adjust marketing priorities at each life-cycle stage to grow or retain market share.

subtopics.title: Market Products Through the Life Cycle

outcomes.text: Describe introduction-stage conditions and marketing focused on building awareness and initial demand.
Describe growth-stage conditions and strategies emphasizing differentiation, quality, promotion, and advertising.
Describe maturity-stage conditions and strategies emphasizing loyalty, differentiation, lower prices, and innovation.
Describe decline-stage conditions and strategies involving cost reduction, redesign, or discontinuation.
Develop and evaluate a pricing strategy.
Explain how pricing affects customer attraction, retention, revenue, profit, and business viability.
Explain why price must exceed per-unit production and distribution cost for profitability.
Describe value-based pricing as charging according to customers’ perceived product value.
Describe competitive pricing as setting prices relative to rivals, including premium, matching, or lower pricing.
Describe cost-based pricing as setting prices to achieve a desired profit per unit.
Describe penetration pricing as initially setting a low price to attract customers and rapidly gain market share.
Evaluate how market conditions affect a business’s pricing power.
Explain how competition and product differentiation influence pricing power.
Explain why highly price-responsive customers limit pricing power and may reduce revenue after price changes.
Explain how price elasticity measures customer responsiveness and constrains price increases.
Describe legal constraints that limit pricing power.
Explain that collusion among competitors to establish prices is illegal in many jurisdictions.
Explain that raising prices excessively during crises, known as price gouging, is illegal in many places.
Explain that price discrimination based on protected characteristics is illegal.
Identify the marketing channels businesses can use to make products available to customers.
Place describes where and how customers obtain products, including stores, memberships, and online locations.
Marketing or distribution channels are the final supply-chain stage connecting finished products with customers.
B2C businesses use channels such as websites and stores, while B2B businesses use channels such as industrial distributors.
Direct channels reach customers without intermediaries; indirect channels use intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers.
Some products, including medicines and hazardous goods, must legally use particular distribution channels.
Choose and assess possible marketing channels for a product.
Compare channels by cost, profitability, customer experience, and ability to reach target customers.
Direct channels offer control over prices and customer experience but may cost more, reach fewer customers, and require specialized expertise.
Indirect channels can lower costs and expand reach through partners’ expertise, but rivals may control distributors or retail space.
Create or assess a coordinated marketing campaign.
A marketing campaign coordinates promotional activities that encourage potential customers to consider a product.
The promotional mix includes media advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, direct marketing, and public relations.
Businesses match promotional tools to customers’ decision processes, using personalized information for significant purchases and broad messages for routine ones.
Media advertising reaches many customers simultaneously with a consistent message through outlets such as television, radio, newspapers, or billboards.
Personal selling provides detailed information or demonstrations, often using a brief value-focused sales presentation.
Sales promotions such as discounts and coupons speed purchasing decisions or help clear excess inventory.
Direct marketing uses materials such as flyers and brochures to deliver targeted messages to many prospects.
Public relations builds a favorable public image rather than directly promoting a particular sale.
Explain how digital marketing tools have transformed business-customer interactions.
Digital marketing uses internet-based tools to connect with customers; businesses increasingly shifted resources from traditional advertising to digital platforms.
Digital tools provide more personalized, lower-cost access to global audiences and targeted customer groups.
Digital marketing generates extensive customer-response data, unlike many traditional methods such as television advertising and billboards.

units.title: UNIT 3: PART 1: Personal Saving and Borrowing

outcomes.text: Explain why consumers save and identify obstacles that can prevent saving.
Consumers earn income from employment and other sources, then spend it on products meeting problems, needs, and wants.
Consumers save for major future purchases, emergencies, and retirement income.
Saving creates an asset and may earn interest determined by rates, savings amount, account type, and economic conditions.
Automated savings, retirement plans, and health savings accounts can encourage saving through convenience or tax advantages.
Irregular income, excessive recurring expenses, instant gratification, lifestyle inflation, and impulse buying can hinder saving.
Explain how PESTEL factors affect savings’ value and incentives to save.
Economic stability, income changes, and living costs influence how much disposable income individuals can save.
Inflation reduces savings’ purchasing power and may discourage people from saving.
Tax policies can encourage saving through tax benefits for designated retirement, healthcare, childcare, or other accounts.
Financial regulations protect savers and support the stability of banks and credit unions.
Develop or assess a savings plan.
Savings amounts depend on personal goals, income, expenses, and the barriers an individual faces.
Choose savings vehicles based on savings amount, goals, time horizon, PESTEL effects, and institutional costs and benefits.
Evaluate institutions and accounts using rates, fees, minimum deposits, risk, location, convenience, reputation, and associated tradeoffs.
Savings accounts are generally insured, interest-bearing deposit accounts whose rates, fees, and minimums vary by institution.
Money market accounts are insured savings vehicles that may require larger deposits, charge higher fees, pay more interest, and offer easier cash access.
Certificates of deposit usually offer higher interest but restrict withdrawals for a fixed period and may require larger deposits.
Checking accounts support frequent transactions; consumers compare fees, access, convenience, and interest when selecting them.
Mobile payment and cryptocurrency accounts may be convenient or appreciate, but generally lack federal insurance and interest.
Explain why consumers borrow and identify available funding sources.
Consumers borrow for purchases exceeding current resources, emergencies, savings preservation, or convenience.
Loans create debt repaid with interest; rates and terms depend on lenders, loan type, amount, and credit history.
Banks and credit unions use deposited funds to make loans to consumers and organizations.
Credit card companies, retailers, mortgage lenders, and alternative financial services also provide consumer loans.
Consumer-protection laws require clear credit terms, regulate collections, and prohibit discriminatory lending.
Explain how lenders assess a prospective borrower’s creditworthiness.
Lenders prefer borrowers with lower risk and charge higher rates to compensate for greater default risk.
Lenders review income, savings, debt, and credit reports when judging creditworthiness.
Credit bureaus compile reports from consumers’ financial interactions with institutions.
Credit reports contain scores and may be provided to lenders, employers, landlords, insurers, and government agencies.
Recommend ways to manage existing debt or use credit.
High debt reduces money available for saving and other expenses; larger balances or rates increase monthly payments.
Income loss or unaffordable monthly payments can make loan repayment difficult.
Maintain strong credit, seek improved loan terms, and quickly repay high-interest debt to reduce debt’s financial impact.
Improve credit scores by paying bills promptly, reducing debt, and limiting credit-card use.
Compare lenders and make down payments to obtain lower loan rates and fees.
Debt management assistance or bankruptcy may help address severe debt, including property seizure or unmanageable repayment obligations.

units.title: UNIT 3: PART 2: Business Finance and Accounting

outcomes.text: Explain why businesses and consumers track and evaluate financial data.
Businesses’ transactions affect their assets, liabilities, and owners’ equity.
Consumers’ income, purchases, savings, and borrowing affect assets, liabilities, and net worth.
Businesses record transactions and prepare reports to monitor performance, guide decisions, inform stakeholders, and comply with regulations.
GAAP requires publicly traded corporations to consistently disclose positive and negative financial information.
Consumers benefit from organized financial tracking, such as budgeting, even though reporting is usually not required.
Describe accounting and finance departments’ roles in preparing, reporting, and using financial information.
Accounting departments record transactions and prepare financial statements.
Managerial accountants analyze information for internal planning and decision making.
Financial accountants provide information mainly to shareholders, investors, and lenders.
Finance departments analyze accounting data and recommend ways to improve financial performance.
Consumers may use financial advisors or accountants for planning, decisions, and tax preparation.
Determine the startup costs of launching a new business or product.
Startup costs include one-time expenditures and initial expenses incurred while establishing a business or product.
One-time expenditures may include legal, incorporation, licensing, and equipment costs.
Initial expenses include occupancy, development, marketing, insurance, and initial inventory costs that later become ongoing.
Describe expenses associated with operating a business.
Classify recurring business costs as direct costs or indirect operating expenses.
Classify recurring costs as fixed or variable based on how they respond to production or service levels.
COGS includes production materials, supplies, labor, benefits, and manufacturing facility costs.
Service businesses’ direct costs include labor, travel, and materials used to deliver services.
Operating expenses include occupancy, staff compensation, marketing, supplies, utilities, maintenance, and insurance.
Insurance protects businesses and consumers from losses, with coverage choices influenced by requirements and risk tolerance.
Explain why businesses seek external financial capital.
Entrepreneurs may fund startups through personal savings, bank loans, or personal credit.
Entrepreneurs compare personal funds with startup needs and calculate sales required to break even.
Businesses seek external capital when they cannot cover startup and operating costs until reaching break-even.
Established businesses seek capital for product development, asset replacement, or increased sales and revenue.
Businesses seek capital to manage cash flow when revenue collection is irregular but expenses remain due.
Determine potential sources of financial capital for a business.
Most business financing comes through loans or equity financing.
New businesses often use friends’ and family’s loans or sell ownership shares.
Established businesses with proven revenue may obtain business bank loans.
Corporations can raise funds by issuing bonds or shares of stock.
Describe potential benefits and risks to lenders and investors providing business capital.
Lenders and investors receive financial assets that can be resold in secondary markets.
Lenders earn interest, including from bonds; corporate bond purchasers become business lenders.
Stock investors may receive dividends, while corporations may retain earnings instead.
Selling an asset above its purchase price produces a capital gain; asset prices respond to several forces.
Calculate annual investment return by dividing total gains by the asset’s price.
Poor business performance can cause lenders and investors to lose income, asset value, or invested capital.
Risk tolerance differs among funders, and riskier investments generally require higher expected returns.
Develop and evaluate funding pitches for prospective lenders or investors.
A funding pitch summarizes a business plan, value proposition, market research, strategy, projections, request, return, and risk.
Funders use reports, projections, and industry data to estimate business valuation and loan repayment capacity.
Funding proposals improve when they demonstrate product-market fit and support financial projections.
Funders may assess leadership qualifications and alignment between the business mission, value proposition, and their goals.
Identify and explain the components of a business income statement.
An income statement compares revenue and costs over time to determine net profit or loss.
Income statements organize information into revenue, cost of goods sold, operating expenses, interest, taxes, and unusual expenses.
Revenue is income generated through a business’s primary activities, such as selling goods or services.
Gross profit equals revenue minus the direct production costs represented by cost of goods sold.
Operating expenses are indirect costs, including selling, administrative, and research and development expenses.
Operating profit equals gross profit minus operating expenses and shows income before interest and taxes.
Interest expense is borrowing cost, and pretax income equals operating profit minus interest expense.
Businesses with positive pretax income record and pay taxes on that income.
Net profit equals pretax income minus taxes and represents the owners’ earnings for the period.
Evaluate business financial performance using information from income statements.
Stakeholders use income statements to track revenue and cost trends, assess profitability, and guide improvement decisions.
Gross profit margin, gross profit divided by revenue, assesses pricing and management of direct costs.
Operating profit margin assesses marketing, sales, administration, and control of operating expenses.
Net profit margin, net profit divided by revenue, measures overall profitability and owners’ income share.
Businesses compare profit margins with forecasts, historical results, and competitors to judge performance.
Use percentage change to calculate rates of change in income, costs, profits, or margins.
Explain why businesses and consumers forecast and plan future income and expenses.
Changing needs, wants, competition, and external forces create financial uncertainty; planning supports financial goals.
Businesses use projected income statements and budgets to estimate revenues, expenses, and profit or loss.
Business budgets help anticipate costs, identify funding requirements, and maintain cash for obligations.
Consumer budgets allocate expected after-tax income among savings, expenses, and debt payments.
Budgets reveal spending habits and help consumers manage debt, save, and support charitable causes while pursuing goals.
Develop an actual or projected income statement for a business.
Use recorded revenues, expenses, and taxes to prepare an income statement.
Forecast revenues, expenses, and taxes to prepare a projected income statement.
Estimate future revenue using pricing plans, customer-demand research, and industry trends.
Estimate COGS and operating expenses from production plans, supply-chain costs, and anticipated business expenses.

topics.title: 3.7 The Balance Sheet and Net Worth

outcomes.text: Identify and explain the components of a business balance sheet.
A balance sheet compares assets, liabilities, and owners’ equity at a specific time; assets equal liabilities plus equity.
Balance-sheet assets are grouped by liquidity as current, long-term, or intangible assets.
Liabilities are business obligations classified as current or long-term according to when payment is due.
Owners’ equity equals assets minus liabilities and commonly includes stock and retained earnings.
Balance sheets commonly compare current financial data with figures from earlier periods.
Interpret information presented on a business balance sheet.
Managers, owners, lenders, and investors use balance sheets to assess financial condition at a particular time.
A balance sheet shows net worth, working-capital sufficiency, and whether debt is reasonable compared with similar businesses.
Insufficient current assets may cause shutdown or bankruptcy, a legal process for liquidation, repayment, or reorganization.
Describe why people determine personal net worth.
Household net worth equals all assets, including savings, investments, property, and possessions, minus liabilities.
Lenders may request household net-worth information during a consumer loan application.
Consumers and financial planners use net worth to assess retirement savings sufficiency.
Identify and explain the components of a business cash-flow statement.
A cash-flow statement shows how cash inflows and outflows change the cash balance during a reporting period.
Businesses monitor cash balances to pay regular expenses, lenders, and unexpected costs.
Cash inflows include customer payments, investment returns, asset sales, and new financial capital.
Cash outflows include payments to workers and suppliers, interest, taxes, asset purchases, debt repayment, and dividends.
A business can end a reporting period with either positive or negative cash flow.
Explain how stakeholders use information from a business cash-flow statement.
Stakeholders use cash flow to judge whether a business can meet obligations to employees, suppliers, creditors, and shareholders.
Negative cash flow can threaten operations despite positive income; businesses may raise funds, collect receivables, or negotiate supplier terms.
Explain why individuals or businesses may have incentives to use unethical financial management or reporting practices.
Recognize unethical financial practices, including fund misuse, tax evasion, embezzlement, bribery, opacity, and falsified statements.
Explain how access to substantial business cash can tempt individuals to steal funds, misuse money, or falsify information.
Explain how misrepresenting financial conditions can affect stock prices, loan terms, or tax obligations.
Explain how laws and professional standards promote ethical conduct among accounting and financial professionals.
Identify financial misconduct that is generally illegal, while recognizing that laws and penalties differ across countries.
Explain how U.S. public-company audits and financial-market rules promote accurate information and protect investors from fraud.
Describe how accounting and finance organizations use ethics codes emphasizing honesty, integrity, transparency, objectivity, and confidentiality.
Explain how internal controls, including conduct codes, audits, and cash-handling procedures, help prevent unethical business behavior.
Describe management as coordinating resources and activities to achieve business goals.
Management plans, organizes, leads, and evaluates human, financial, and physical resources to meet objectives.
Managers at every organizational level make decisions and lead business activities.
Department managers coordinate employees’ work so it supports the business vision and mission.
Identify and demonstrate effective leadership and business communication abilities.
Effective leaders communicate and collaborate with supervisors, employees, customers, investors, lenders, and other stakeholders.
Leadership includes expressing vision, building teams, resolving conflict, and motivating people.
Strong communication involves clarity, persuasion, empathetic listening, and appropriately responding to feedback.
Explain why businesses hire and develop employees with varied competencies.
Businesses employ people to produce goods, serve customers, market, sell, and manage finances.
Businesses need diverse skills and backgrounds for different tasks, while outsourcing work outside their core activities.
Skilled, trained employees support product quality, customer service, reputation, revenue, and business viability.
Employee development can involve college, apprenticeships, workplace instruction, online courses, and continuing education.
Explain how businesses compensate, motivate, and retain capable employees.
Businesses may hire full-time, part-time, temporary, or contract workers.
Compensation may use wages, salaries, commissions, piece rates, or profit sharing, depending on role, law, industry, and competition.
Employers generally set pay by considering education, skills, and productivity.
Benefits may include health coverage, retirement plans, health savings accounts, disability insurance, education reimbursement, and paid leave.
Raises, promotions, bonuses, autonomy, flexibility, recognition, and workplace culture can motivate and retain employees.
Describe performance indicators used to assess business performance.
A KPI is a measured data point showing performance, goal progress, or strategy effectiveness.
Managers choose KPIs connected to mission, goals, profitability, competitiveness, viability, and industry characteristics.
Develop or interpret financial and nonfinancial KPIs to track financial health and goal progress.
Financial-health KPIs include revenue, profit, margins, costs, expenses, and cash flow.
Marketing and sales KPIs include acquisition cost, customer lifetime value, satisfaction, retention, sales, and market share.
Operations KPIs include unit cost, delivery cost, order accuracy, and on-time delivery rates.
Explain how businesses use benchmarks.
A benchmark is a comparison standard based on historical company data or industry performance.
Businesses compare KPI results with benchmarks to evaluate performance against a recognized standard.
Explain how and why businesses create and use strategies to accomplish goals.
A strategy outlines how a business will pursue goals such as advantage, mission fulfillment, revenue, cost reduction, or profit.
Businesses collect and monitor financial, customer, competitor, and market-trend data to create and adjust strategies.
A clear strategy aligns resources toward goals or challenges, improving the likelihood of success.
Strategy directs decisions and tactics, which are actions intended to advance strategic goals.
Apply a careful, evidence-based process to make business decisions.
The PACED process defines a problem, develops alternatives, establishes criteria, evaluates options, and selects an approach.
Decision criteria consider measurable and intangible costs and benefits, including effects on profits, reputation, mission, and values.
Criteria may address ROI, competitiveness, supply-chain risk, operating effects, and impacts on employees.
Strategic frameworks systematically compare internal and external factors against long-term goals and strategy.
Managers may need to rank conflicting criteria when information is limited or imperfect.

topics.title: 4.4 Strategic Frameworks: Porter’s Five Forces and SWOT Analysis

outcomes.text: Describe Porter’s Five Forces framework.
Porter’s Five Forces evaluates competitive intensity, market attractiveness, and potential profitability.
The five forces are rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, customer power, and supplier power.
Competitive rivalry depends on the number of rivals, product differentiation, and businesses’ pricing power.
The threat of new entrants reflects how easily competitors can enter, based on barriers to entry.
Substitute threats arise when alternative products or services can satisfy the same customer needs.
Customer power is buyers’ ability to pressure prices, influenced by customer numbers, acquisition costs, and switching costs.
Supplier power is providers’ ability to increase input costs, influenced by resource-market competitiveness.
Use Porter’s Five Forces to judge how competitive a market is.
Strong competitive forces make markets less attractive and reduce potential profitability; weak forces have the opposite effect.
Assess rivalry by examining direct competitors, product differentiation, and businesses’ pricing power.
Assess new-entry threats by examining entry barriers and how easily newcomers can compete for market share.
Assess substitute threats by considering the availability, price, accessibility, and quality of alternative products.
Assess customer power using customer concentration, sales significance, acquisition costs, and switching costs.
Assess supplier power using the number of providers and the costs of changing suppliers.
Explain SWOT factors used to evaluate business viability.
SWOT evaluates internal and external factors affecting a business’s ability to achieve goals and compete.
The four SWOT categories are strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
Strengths are internal advantages, including competencies, reputation, quality, resources, employees, and supply-chain efficiency.
Weaknesses are internal disadvantages, such as capability gaps, poor quality, limited resources, staffing problems, or outdated systems.
Opportunities are external conditions that could help a business, including growth, less competition, technological progress, or favorable regulation.
Threats are external conditions that could harm a business, including higher costs, disasters, regulation, or disruptive innovation.
Use SWOT analysis to evaluate internal capabilities, external opportunities, and external threats.
Evaluate internal resources and intangible assets against rivals, benchmarks, past results, and external conditions to identify strengths or weaknesses.
Evaluate market size, customer preferences, PESTEL factors, and competitive forces to identify favorable external conditions.
Use SWOT findings to build strengths, correct weaknesses, pursue opportunities, and address threats.

units.title: UNIT 5: Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing

outcomes.text: Retirement choices depend on preferences, health, well-being, and funding; income may combine Social Security, employer plans, investments, and continued earnings.
Families sharing finances can reduce conflict by discussing and jointly planning long-term financial goals.
Automatic savings and payroll retirement deductions can help overcome obstacles to saving.
Charitable giving choices reflect personal goals and nonprofit missions; donations may also provide tax advantages.
Describe factors that affect an individual’s or household’s returns from financial assets.
Long-term savers may choose among savings accounts, certificates of deposit, stocks, bonds, and mutual funds.
Starting early and holding investments longer can increase returns through compounding.
Financial assets differ in risk and expected return; safer assets generally offer lower expected returns than riskier assets.
Transaction, management, and advisory fees reduce investment returns; discount brokers generally charge less but provide less advice.
Taxes on interest, dividends, and capital gains reduce investment returns and should influence asset choices.
Inflation lowers purchasing power and therefore reduces an investment’s real, inflation-adjusted return.
Biases such as overconfidence and loss aversion can lead investors to make choices that reduce returns.
Recommend a savings and investment plan considering goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance.
Asset allocation should reflect funding needs, saving capacity, time horizon, risk tolerance, and expected returns.
Longer horizons may justify riskier assets, while shorter horizons generally favor safer assets to reduce downturn losses.
Risk-averse investors often choose insured savings and CDs, whereas risk-tolerant investors may choose stocks and mutual funds.
When selecting financial advisors, consider their licenses, credentials, education, experience, and fees.
Diversification spreads money across assets with varying risks and returns, seeking stronger long-term returns without excessive risk.
Investors often evaluate asset performance by comparing it with benchmarks such as stock or bond indexes.
